newsitem.title: THAILAND: S.Korean woes seen speeding liberalisation.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean woes seen speeding liberalisation.

text.p: South Korea's corporate travails will lead to rapid liberalisation of the country's financial markets in the immediate future, a senior South Korean executive told a conference on Asian Bonds on Tuesday.

"I think the Korean government is fully aware of the fact that financial reform is an absolutely necessary measure and will therefore, speed up forthcoming finance reforms and liberalisation," Insup Lee, the managing director of one of the coutry's largest trusts, Seoul Investment Trust Management Co, told the conference.
Bond market measures to be implemented this year include establishing Korean bond funds in Asia and Europe worth $200 million each, he said.

In addition, South Korean firms will be given more freedom to issue commercial paper offshore, and foreign investors will be allowed to hold a aggregate total of 50 percent of the unsecured bonds of small- and medium-sized companies, he said.
Aggregate foreign ownership of unsecured commercial bills issued by large conglomerates will be raised to 30 percent and individual foreign ownership to six percent, he said.

On-going interest rate reforms will see borrowing costs drop to 11 percent by year end. Current rates around 11.50 percent and short-term liquidity restraints, caused by the demands of some struggling conglomerates, could maintain upward presure on rates in the short term, Lee said.
South Korea has seen a series of large corporate failures this year, which began with the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co in January, and distorted money market supply.
"When we have such problems with conglomerates or chaibols, definitely, there will be a credit crunch in the local markets. And that is why, recently, interest rates have not gone down," he said.
But recent interest rate liberalisation will bring benefits in the second half, Lee said.
South Korea is at stage four of a sweeping interest rate deregulation program that recently saw the Bank of Korea allow commercial banks to set their own rates on savings accounts.

The new regulations will affect short-term interest rates on commercial papers, certificates of deposits and repurchase agreements, short-term trust products for investment trust companies, rates on short-term savings deposits at mutual savings and finance companies and credit unions, he said.

In the Korean equity market, foreign ownership limits will be raised to 25-26 percent in the second half of 1997 from the 23 percent, Lee said. The ceiling will be raised to 30 percent in 1998 and 35 percent in 1999 before the market is fully liberalised in 2000, he said. Foreign access to the over-the-counter equity market will also be increased later this year, Lee said.
Further measures include an increase in the permitted levels of overseas borrowing by the state-run Korea Development Bank and Export-Import Bank of Korea, Lee said.
